notes: Infrastructure caveat: isolation:worktree branched every run from 'main' (pre-fix, pre-skill), not from the branch these evals were designed against. With-skill agents still obtained real skill content (several explicitly note reading .claude/skills/soct-add-component/ from the original checkout path since their own worktree lacked it), so the with_skill vs without_skill manipulation itself is intact, but every worktree's underlying repo state is one branch older than intended. Verified by direct on-disk inspection, not just agent self-report.

Eval 'model-critic-wide' is the cleanest signal: with_skill and without_skill produced near-identical structural output, but only with_skill used cfg_utils.cfg_get (3 occurrences) instead of bare dict.get (0 occurrences) in the new model file, the exact convention the skill calls out as the standard for new model code. Same delta reproduced independently in 'model-actor-gaussian-wide-cfg-trap'.

Evals 'agent-delayed-td3', 'buffer-fifo', 'env-circle3d', and 'driver-seed-sweep' scored 100% in both configurations — these tasks' conventions (subclass the obvious sibling, mirror an existing test class, follow an explicit in-prompt naming pattern) were discoverable by a careful agent reading the codebase directly, without needing the skill. This is a ceiling effect worth knowing about, not a flaw in the skill: it means the skill's marginal value concentrates on the genuinely non-obvious conventions (cfg-shape/activation-count rules, cfg_utils.cfg_get, the memory() gotcha, the buffer_type PER-substring gate) rather than on structure a competent agent would infer anyway.

'model-actor-gaussian-wide-cfg-trap' was deliberately primed in its own prompt wording ('we've been bitten before by a silent cfg mismatch') — both configurations got the cfg shape exactly right, including the without_skill run independently finding and fixing the real pre-existing actor_gaussian-v0 bug in its worktree. This suggests the prompt's own wording did much of the work the skill would otherwise provide; a less-hinted version of this eval would likely show a larger gap and is worth adding in a future iteration.

with_skill runs took longer and used more tokens on average (skill files add real reading time), which is an expected, acceptable cost given the pass-rate/convention-adherence gain on the evals that did differentiate.
